Reference solution (PostgreSQL). {{gap_s}} is the session gap in seconds ({{gap_min}} minutes × 60) at Hard and Very Hard; at Medium the generator sets it to −1, so every play starts its own session, which is the Medium rule.

WITH p AS (                              -- previews are not plays (none at Medium)
  SELECT * FROM plays WHERE NOT is_preview
), gaps AS (
  SELECT p.*,
         LAG(stopped_at) OVER (PARTITION BY profile_id, title_id
                               ORDER BY started_at, play_id) AS prev_stop
  FROM p
), numbered AS (                         -- a new session unless it starts within the gap
  SELECT g.*,
         SUM(CASE WHEN prev_stop IS NULL
                    OR started_at > prev_stop + make_interval(secs => {{gap_s}})
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY profile_id, title_id
                 ORDER BY started_at, play_id) AS session_no
  FROM gaps g
), sessions AS (
  SELECT profile_id, title_id, session_no,
         (ARRAY_AGG(country ORDER BY started_at, play_id))[1]          AS country,
         (ARRAY_AGG(start_position_s ORDER BY started_at, play_id))[1] AS first_position_s,
         MAX(end_position_s)                                           AS furthest_s
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY profile_id, title_id, session_no
)
SELECT title_id, country,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS plays,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE furthest_s < {{n_sec}})    AS early_stops,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE furthest_s < {{n_sec}})::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS early_stop_rate
FROM sessions
WHERE first_position_s = 0               -- a resumed session is not a start (Very Hard)
GROUP BY title_id, country
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_plays}}
ORDER BY early_stop_rate DESC, title_id, country;

Explanation. Previews are removed first, because a preview sitting just before a real play would otherwise join its session and change where that session starts. LAG(stopped_at) per profile and title gives the previous play's stop; a play opens a new session when there is no previous play or it starts more than the gap after that stop (exactly the gap still continues the session). A running SUM of those flags numbers the sessions: classic gaps and islands. Each session is then reduced to its country and starting position (from its first play) and its furthest position (MAX(end_position_s), not the last play's end: a viewer who watched 40 minutes and then restarted the opening did not abandon). Resumed sessions (first position not 0) are excluded before counting, so they leave both the numerator and the denominator. The floor is a HAVING COUNT(*) >= floor on the counted sessions, and the rate is a numeric division rounded to 4 places.

Complexity. One sort per (profile, title) partition for the window functions, then two hash aggregates: O(n log n) over plays. In production, sessions are usually built once in a sessionisation job and stored; this query would read the session table.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery: LAG and windowed SUM are the same; use TIMESTAMPADD(second, …) / TIMESTAMP_ADD(… INTERVAL n SECOND), COUNT_IF / COUNTIF, and ARRAY_AGG(…)[OFFSET(0)] (BigQuery) or MIN_BY(start_position_s, started_at) (Snowflake, Databricks SQL) for the first play. Spark SQL: min_by, count_if. MySQL 8: window functions exist; no FILTER, use SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. One title and country with exactly the floor of plays, one of which stops at exactly N minutes (every level); pairs below the floor; a profile restarting a title exactly G minutes and 1 second after stopping (two sessions). Hard: previews; sessions of two or three plays with gaps of exactly G minutes; a rewind (furthest position earlier than the last play's end). Very Hard: resumed sessions that would be early stops and others that would not; a preview immediately followed by a resumed play.

Common mistakes. Wall-clock duration instead of position; <= at N minutes; a strict floor (>); integer division; filtering previews after sessionising; a gap test with >= (splitting at exactly G minutes); the last play's end instead of the maximum; excluding resumed plays rather than resumed sessions; ordering only by the rate.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Parameterise N, add device type to the grouping, and show the floor's effect openly ("hidden: fewer than k plays"); a 30-second threshold mostly measures previews and accidental clicks. (2) Treat "skip intro/recap" and "next episode" actions as their own outcome; per-episode thresholds or position relative to the end of the recap. (3) Sessionise per (profile, title) with state carried across the partition boundary: process day D with the open sessions of D−1, or allow a late window and restate. (4) Compare against a holdout or the same title in countries without the change, check novelty effects, and keep the definition fixed during the test.

NFX-L1-02.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL). {{min_view_minutes}} is 1 below Very Hard (every session has at least one minute, so every viewer counts).

WITH tagged AS (                          -- half-open weeks: [Monday 00:00, next Monday 00:00)
  SELECT s.*,
         CASE WHEN started_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{prev_week_start}} 00:00:00+00'
               AND started_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{week_start}} 00:00:00+00'      THEN 'prev'
              WHEN started_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{week_start}} 00:00:00+00'
               AND started_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{next_week_start}} 00:00:00+00' THEN 'curr'
         END AS wk
  FROM viewing_sessions s
), title_week AS (
  SELECT country, title_id, wk, SUM(minutes_viewed) AS minutes
  FROM tagged WHERE wk IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY country, title_id, wk
), shares AS (                            -- denominator: every title in the country that week
  SELECT country, title_id, wk,
         ROUND(100.0 * minutes / SUM(minutes) OVER (PARTITION BY country, wk), 2) AS pct
  FROM title_week
), viewers AS (                           -- distinct profiles with enough minutes this week
  SELECT country, title_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM (SELECT country, title_id, profile_id
        FROM tagged WHERE wk = 'curr'
        GROUP BY country, title_id, profile_id
        HAVING SUM(minutes_viewed) >= {{min_view_minutes}}) v
  GROUP BY country, title_id
), candidates AS (
  SELECT c.country, c.title_id,
         COALESCE(p.pct, 0)         AS prev_share_pct,
         c.pct                      AS curr_share_pct,
         c.pct - COALESCE(p.pct, 0) AS gain_pts
  FROM shares c
  JOIN viewers v ON v.country = c.country AND v.title_id = c.title_id
  LEFT JOIN shares p ON p.country = c.country AND p.title_id = c.title_id AND p.wk = 'prev'
  WHERE c.wk = 'curr' AND v.n >= {{min_viewers}} AND c.pct - COALESCE(p.pct, 0) > 0
), ranked AS (
  SELECT candidates.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY gain_pts DESC) AS gain_rank
  FROM candidates
)
SELECT country, title_id, prev_share_pct, curr_share_pct, gain_pts, gain_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE gain_rank <= {{top_k}}
ORDER BY country, gain_rank, title_id;

Explanation. Each session is tagged with its week using half-open ranges, so a session at exactly Monday 00:00:00 belongs only to the week that starts then and sessions outside the two weeks drop out. Minutes are summed per (country, title, week); a window SUM over (country, week) gives the denominator from all titles, which is why the share is computed before any candidate filter. Viewers come from the raw current-week sessions grouped by profile, so a profile counts once and, at Very Hard, only if its minutes summed over sessions reach the minimum. The current week is LEFT-joined to the previous one with COALESCE(…, 0), so titles that are new this week keep their whole share as gain. Candidates must meet the threshold and have a strictly positive gain; RANK() keeps ties and skips the following rank, and the filter gain_rank <= K keeps everyone tied at the cut-off.

Complexity. A scan and hash aggregate of the sessions, a small window over (country, title, week) rows, and a sort per country for the rank: O(n) plus O(t log t) for t titles. The distinct-viewer count is the expensive part at scale.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(DATE(started_at), WEEK(MONDAY)) — its default week starts on Sunday; COUNT(DISTINCT …) is exact, APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT is HyperLogLog-based. Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('week', …) depends on the WEEK_START session parameter; QUALIFY RANK() … <= K. Spark SQL: date_trunc('week', …) starts on Monday; approx_count_distinct. MySQL 8: RANK() in a derived table; WEEKDAY() arithmetic for Monday weeks.

Edge cases built into the data. Two titles with identical minutes in both weeks (an exact tie); a title not viewed last week; a title with exactly the threshold of viewers; a title with a big rise but one viewer short, one of whose viewers came back twice more (sessions are not viewers). Hard: sessions at Monday 00:00:00 and Sunday 23:59:59, and sessions in the weeks before and after, including the next Monday 00:00:00. Very Hard: light viewers below the minute minimum, a viewer reaching exactly the minimum over two sessions, and a title that qualifies only if light viewers count.

Common mistakes. Ranking raw minutes or the ratio of shares; computing shares over candidates only; an inner join that drops new titles; ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK; COUNT(*) of sessions for viewers; BETWEEN week bounds; comparing started_at::date to a Sunday without considering the time zone; applying the minute minimum per session instead of per viewer.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Convert to each country's local time before deciding the week (countries with several time zones need a rule); sessions near local midnight between Sunday and Monday move weeks, and the cut-off differs by country. (2) Approximate counts are fine for ranking well above the threshold but not for the threshold itself; count exactly for titles near it, or publish with a margin. (3) Compare a launch against a baseline that accounts for days available (minutes per day since launch) or wait for a full week; state the rule. (4) Freeze a week's result at a defined cut-off, record late data separately, and publish restatements explicitly with a version.

Rubric anchors. 2: shares and gains right, but ties handled with ROW_NUMBER, new titles dropped, or the denominator filtered. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles local weeks, approximate distinct counts and restatements convincingly.

Strong signals. Asks whether the denominator includes non-candidates; checks the tie rule before choosing a ranking function. Red flags. Averaging daily shares into a weekly share; "the top K is always K rows".

NFX-L1-03.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL). {{as_of}} is the snapshot time; below Very Hard no stream is open and no device overlaps itself, so the COALESCE and COUNT(DISTINCT device_id) change nothing.

WITH s AS (                               -- an open stream runs until the snapshot
  SELECT account_id, device_id, started_at,
         COALESCE(ended_at, TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}') AS ended_at
  FROM streams
), pieces AS (                            -- one piece per UTC day the stream covers, [start, end)
  SELECT s.account_id, s.device_id, d::date AS stream_date,
         GREATEST(s.started_at, d)                AS p_start,
         LEAST(s.ended_at, d + INTERVAL '1 day')  AS p_end
  FROM s
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(date_trunc('day', s.started_at),
                                     s.ended_at - INTERVAL '1 microsecond',
                                     INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
), concurrency AS (                       -- devices playing at each piece's start
  SELECT a.account_id, a.stream_date, a.p_start,
         COUNT(DISTINCT b.device_id) AS playing
  FROM pieces a
  JOIN pieces b
    ON b.account_id = a.account_id
   AND b.stream_date = a.stream_date
   AND b.p_start <= a.p_start AND a.p_start < b.p_end
  GROUP BY a.account_id, a.stream_date, a.p_start
), peaks AS (
  SELECT account_id, stream_date, MAX(playing) AS peak
  FROM concurrency
  GROUP BY account_id, stream_date
)
SELECT pk.stream_date, pl.plan_name,
       COUNT(*)     AS accounts_over_limit,
       MAX(pk.peak) AS peak_streams
FROM peaks pk
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = pk.account_id
JOIN plans pl   ON pl.plan_id = a.plan_id
WHERE pk.peak > pl.max_streams
GROUP BY pk.stream_date, pl.plan_name
ORDER BY pk.stream_date, pl.plan_name;

Explanation. An open stream is closed at the snapshot time. Every stream is cut into one piece per UTC day it covers, clipped to that day; ending the series at ended_at − 1 µs keeps a stream that ends at exactly midnight off the next day. Concurrency only rises when a piece starts, and a piece of a stream already playing at midnight starts at 00:00:00, so evaluating each piece's start covers every instant where a peak can occur, including the carry-over into the new day. At each such instant the self join counts the devices whose piece covers it, with the half-open test start <= t < end. The peak per (account, day) is compared strictly with the plan's limit, and the over-limit accounts are counted and their peaks maximised per (day, plan).

Complexity. The day split multiplies rows by the days covered (about 1). The self join is O(k²) per (account, day) for k pieces; with k small it is fine. A sweep (SUM(+1/−1) OVER (PARTITION BY account, day ORDER BY t, delta) with −1 before +1 at equal t) is O(k log k) and the better answer at scale.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: GENERATE_TIMESTAMP_ARRAY or GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY with UNNEST for the day split; TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(…, DAY). Snowflake: no generate_series; join to a calendar table or TABLE(GENERATOR(…)) with DATEADD. Spark SQL: explode(sequence(to_date(started_at), to_date(ended_at - INTERVAL 1 MICROSECOND))). MySQL 8: a recursive CTE or a calendar table; GREATEST/LEAST exist.

Edge cases built into the data. For every level: two accounts on different plans over the limit; an account whose (limit + 1)-th stream starts exactly when another ends (not over); plans whose limits vary by seed. Hard: an account over the limit on both sides of midnight with every stream started before midnight; one whose crossing stream only becomes a problem after midnight; one whose streams all end at exactly 00:00:00. Very Hard: a device that reconnected while its old row was still open (one stream); a stream with ended_at NULL that pushes an account over the limit before the snapshot.

Common mistakes. Inclusive ends (<= or BETWEEN); >= against the limit; assigning a stream only to the day it started; evaluating only at stream starts without the midnight pieces; ended_at::date making a midnight end count on the next day; counting rows instead of devices; dropping open streams; computing peaks per plan without going through accounts.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Replace the self join with an event sweep per account and day; at scale, partition by account. (2) Per-account state of active devices with heartbeats and a lease (a device that stops sending heartbeats for n seconds is released); start requests check and reserve atomically; decide the behaviour when the state store is unavailable (fail open or closed, and say why). (3) Use server-side timestamps for start and stop, or correct with the measured skew; treat device times as untrusted. (4) Re-run the same computation with the lower limit; it shows how often accounts reached a level, not whether people would have changed behaviour under a different plan.

Rubric anchors. 2: right structure but closed intervals, >=, or start-day attribution. 3: matches the expected result at the level attempted. 4: also proposes the sweep, a sound real-time design and clock handling.

Strong signals. Draws two intervals touching end to start and asks what counts; explains why the peak is reached at a start. Red flags. Sampling the timeline every minute; claiming the result describes how a real service enforces its plans.

def fill_rows(rows, cap, min_fill, genres=None, row_genre_cap=None, page_genre_cap=None):
    order = sorted(range(len(rows)), key=lambda i: (-rows[i][1], rows[i][0]))
    on_page = set()                    # titles in rows kept so far
    page_genre = {}                    # genre -> titles of it in kept rows
    kept = {}
    for i in order:
        got, in_row, row_genre = [], set(), {}
        for t in rows[i][2]:
            if len(got) == cap:
                break
            if t in on_page or t in in_row:
                continue
            if genres is not None:
                g = genres[t]
                if row_genre_cap is not None and row_genre.get(g, 0) >= row_genre_cap:
                    continue           # skipped for this row only
                if page_genre_cap is not None and page_genre.get(g, 0) + row_genre.get(g, 0) >= page_genre_cap:
                    continue
                row_genre[g] = row_genre.get(g, 0) + 1
            got.append(t)
            in_row.add(t)
        if len(got) >= min_fill:       # commit only kept rows: a dropped row releases everything
            kept[i] = got
            on_page |= in_row
            for g, n in row_genre.items():
                page_genre[g] = page_genre.get(g, 0) + n
    return [(rows[i][0], kept[i]) for i in range(len(rows)) if i in kept]

Explanation. Rows are filled in (-priority, row_id) order but returned in their input order, so the function needs both orderings. Each row is built in local structures (got, in_row, row_genre) and committed to the page-level set and genre counter only if it is kept; a dropped row therefore releases its titles and its genre budget without any undo logic. A title skipped because of a genre limit is only skipped for that row, since nothing about it is recorded. Membership and counting are O(1) with a set and dictionaries.

Complexity. O(R log R) to order the rows plus O(total candidates) to scan them; memory O(titles on the page). In the timing check (3 000 rows × 150 candidates) the reference takes well under a second in CPython; a version that checks "already on the page" by scanning a list of placed titles takes minutes.

Dialect notes. In Java or Go, a HashSet<Integer>/map[int]struct{} and a per-genre int array if genres are small integers; sort row indices with a comparator on (priority desc, row id). In SQL this greedy, order-dependent fill is awkward (each row depends on all earlier rows); it belongs in application code. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A title already in a higher-priority row; repeats within a row; fill order differing from display order; equal priorities; a dropped row whose titles go to a later row; exactly min_fill; a row stopping at cap with later candidates left for others; no row kept ([]); an empty candidate list. Hard: a title skipped for the genre cap and taken by a later row; a genre cap that drops a row below min_fill. Very Hard: the page genre cap counted across kept rows, released by a dropped row, and reached exactly.

Common mistakes. Returning rows in fill order; marking titles as used before knowing the row is kept; marking genre-skipped titles as used; a list for membership; forgetting duplicates within a row; > instead of >= for min_fill; sorting by priority ascending or breaking ties by display position.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A page-level assignment (titles to slots, maximising total relevance with one-title-per-page constraints) is a matching or integer programme; usually not worth it per request, but useful offline to measure how much greedy loses. (2) Precompute candidate lists per profile or segment, keep a per-row timeout with a fallback row, and assemble with whatever arrived. (3) Deduplicate on the visible prefix only, or weight positions; state the rule and test it. (4) Replay a sample of profiles through old and new assemblers and alert on distribution changes in rows kept and titles per row.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct for simple pages but returns fill order or leaks dropped rows' titles; or correct but list-based and too slow. 3: passes all tests at the level attempted within the time limit. 4: also discusses the optimum, latency and offline testing well.

def repair_cues(cues, num, den, offset_ms, min_gap_ms, dedupe=False):
    def rescale(t):
        return (2 * t * num + den) // (2 * den)       # round half up, integers only

    moved = []
    for i, (s, e, text) in enumerate(cues):
        ns, ne = rescale(s) + offset_ms, rescale(e) + offset_ms
        if ne <= 0:
            continue                                  # entirely before the programme starts
        moved.append((max(ns, 0), i, ne, text))
    moved.sort()                                      # by new start, then input position

    merged = []                                       # [start, end, lines, seen]
    for s, _, e, text in moved:
        if merged and s < merged[-1][1]:              # strict overlap: touching is not merging
            cur = merged[-1]
            cur[1] = max(cur[1], e)
            if dedupe and text in cur[3]:
                continue
            cur[2].append(text)
            cur[3].add(text)
        else:
            merged.append([s, e, [text], {text}])

    for a, b in zip(merged, merged[1:]):              # close gaps shorter than min_gap_ms
        if 0 < b[0] - a[1] < min_gap_ms:
            a[1] = b[0]
    return [(s, e, "\n".join(lines)) for s, e, lines, _ in merged]

Explanation. Every time is rescaled with integer arithmetic: (2·t·num + den) // (2·den) is t·num/den rounded half up, with no float that could land just below .5 (and no banker's rounding from round()). The offset is added after rescaling; a cue whose new end is at or before 0 is dropped, and a negative start is clamped to 0. Sorting by (new_start, input_position) makes equal starts keep input order. One sweep merges: a cue joins the current merged cue when it starts strictly before that cue's end (the maximum end so far, which handles chains and a cue nested inside another); otherwise it starts a new merged cue. With dedupe, a line already in the merged cue is skipped (a set beside the list). from collections import OrderedDict


def edge_cache(requests, capacity, admit_on_second=False):
    cache = OrderedDict()           # object_id -> (version, size); the first entry is the least recently used
    used = 0
    seen = set()
    hits = hit_bytes = total = 0
    for oid, ver, size in requests:
        total += size
        cur = cache.get(oid)
        if cur is not None and cur[0] == ver:
            hits += 1
            hit_bytes += size
            cache.move_to_end(oid)
        else:
            if cur is not None:                       # a stale version: drop it before anything else
                del cache[oid]
                used -= cur[1]
            if size <= capacity and (not admit_on_second or oid in seen):
                while used + size > capacity:
                    _, (_, s) = cache.popitem(last=False)
                    used -= s
                cache[oid] = (ver, size)
                used += size
        seen.add(oid)
    return (hits, hit_bytes, total)

Explanation. An ordered dictionary keyed by object_id keeps the segments in recency order: move_to_end on a hit, popitem(last=False) to evict the least recently used one. A running byte total replaces any summing. On a miss, a cached copy at another version is removed first. That has to happen before the admission decision, because the stale copy must go even when the new version is too large to store. Then the oversized check, then admission, then eviction until the new segment fits. The seen set records every request, so with admit_on_second the first request of a segment is served from upstream and not stored, and its second request is admitted even if it is a different version. The function returns integers, so the result is exact.

Complexity. O(1) amortised per request: each segment is inserted once per admission and evicted at most once, so the eviction loop is amortised over insertions. O(cached segments + distinct ids) memory. The timing test (300 000 requests, 60 000 segments, about 13 000 cached) runs in about 0.4 s in CPython. A Python list kept in recency order needs list.remove on every hit, which is O(cached) and took about 20 s. Scanning a dictionary of last-use stamps for the minimum on every eviction took more than a minute.

Dialect notes. In Java, a LinkedHashMap with access order gives the same structure; removeEldestEntry evicts at most one entry per insertion, so for bytes keep an explicit eviction loop. In C++, std::list plus an unordered_map from id to list iterator. In Scala, a mutable.LinkedHashMap with remove-and-reinsert on a hit. Byte totals need 64-bit integers. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An empty trace; a segment of exactly capacity bytes stored and evicting everything; a segment one byte larger never stored and evicting nothing; a hit refreshing recency; one large segment evicting several small ones, oldest first; a segment fitting exactly after earlier ones without eviction; capacity 0; hits counted in requests and bytes. (Hard) the first request never stored with admit_on_second; a request that was not stored still counting as seen; a one-hit segment never evicting a cached one; an oversized segment not stored on its second request; the same trace with the flag off. (Very Hard) a new version replacing the old copy; the stale copy dropped even when the new version is too large; an older version after a newer one; a new version counting as a repeat for admission; a larger new version evicting others.

Common mistakes. size < capacity instead of <=; evicting before checking that the segment can fit at all, which empties the cache for an oversized segment; forgetting to refresh recency on a hit; recording seen only for admitted segments; keeping the stale version when the new one is not admitted; treating any cached copy as a hit regardless of version; returning a float ratio; an O(n) list or a min-scan for eviction.

Follow-up guidance. (1) For unit sizes, one pass computing each request's stack distance gives the hit ratio at every capacity at once (Mattson's algorithm). With variable sizes, the distance is the bytes of distinct segments requested since the last request of this one: in pure LRU by bytes, a request hits at capacity C when that distance plus its own size is at most C, apart from segments too large to store, which need care. The distances come from one pass with a Fenwick tree over request positions. Admission breaks the single-pass trick. (2) Second-request admission keeps one-hit segments from evicting useful ones. It lowers the ratio on traces where most segments are requested exactly twice and close together, because every second request is now a miss. (3) Windowed or segmented LRU, frequency with decay, or an admission filter such as a small sketch; compare policies on the same trace, including a warm-up period excluded from the ratio, and report bytes and requests. (4) Sharding by a consistent hash of the segment id, per-disk LRU, and a memory tier in front; the simulator models each shard as its own cache and the hashing as a router.

def prune_ladder(encodes, max_rungs=None):
    by_title = {}
    for title, enc_id, kbps, quality in encodes:
        if quality is None:
            continue
        pts = by_title.setdefault(title, {})
        key = (kbps, quality)
        if key not in pts or enc_id < pts[key]:      # exact duplicates: the smallest id
            pts[key] = enc_id

    def cross(a, p, c):                               # > 0 when p is strictly above the line a-c
        return (c[0] - a[0]) * (p[1] - a[1]) - (c[1] - a[1]) * (p[0] - a[0])

    out = {}
    for title, pts in by_title.items():
        # by bitrate, the best score first at each bitrate
        order = sorted(pts, key=lambda bq: (bq[0], -bq[1]))
        hull = []
        best_q = None
        for p in order:
            if best_q is not None and p[1] <= best_q:   # same or higher bitrate, no better score
                continue
            best_q = p[1]
            while len(hull) >= 2 and cross(hull[-2], hull[-1], p) <= 0:
                hull.pop()                              # on or below the new chord
            hull.append(p)
        if max_rungs is not None:
            while len(hull) > max_rungs:
                i = min(range(1, len(hull) - 1), key=lambda j: (cross(hull[j - 1], hull[j], hull[j + 1]), j))
                del hull[i]
        out[title] = [pts[p] for p in hull]
    return out

Explanation. One pass groups the scored encodes by title and resolves exact duplicates to the smallest id in a dictionary keyed by (bitrate, quality). Each title's points are sorted by bitrate, highest score first at equal bitrates. Walking that order, any point whose score is not above the best so far is dominated, because something at an equal or lower bitrate already scored at least as much; that also stops the ladder at the lowest bitrate that reaches the best score. The remaining points rise in both coordinates, and a monotone stack keeps the upper hull: a point is popped while it lies on or below the chord from the rung under it to the new point. The test is an integer cross product, and <= 0 drops collinear points. For a rung budget, the interior rung with the smallest triangle (twice its area is the same cross product) is removed, ties to the lower bitrate, and the neighbours' areas are recomputed after each removal.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sorts, O(n) for the stacks. With a budget, the reference rescans the interior rungs after each removal, O(h²) per title for a ladder of h rungs, which is cheap because ladders are short. A heap with lazy invalidation and a linked list gives O(h log h) for long ladders. The timing test (360 000 encodes, 12 000 titles, interleaved) runs in about 1 s in CPython. Testing every chord for every encode (O(n³) per title) took about 17 s, and filtering the full input once per title is O(titles × n) and does not finish.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ use 64-bit integers for the cross product: bitrate differences of 16 000 times score differences of 10 000 already reach 1.6 × 10⁸, and larger units would overflow 32 bits. A SQL version can do the dominance step with a window MAX(quality) OVER (PARTITION BY title ORDER BY bitrate ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING), but the hull itself needs a stack and is not natural in SQL; a Spark job would group by title and run the stack in a per-group function. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A single encode; an encode exactly on a chord (dropped); one point above it (kept); an encode below a chord; a dominated encode; two encodes at one bitrate; the best score reached at two bitrates; interleaved titles. (Hard) exact duplicates resolved by string comparison ("e1032" < "e417"); an encode with no score; a title with no scored encodes left out; three collinear encodes in a longer ladder. (Very Hard) a budget at least the ladder's length; the smallest triangle removed first; neighbours changing after each removal; a budget of 2; equal areas removing the lower bitrate; the budget applied per title.

Common mistakes. Comparing slopes with floating-point division, which can keep a collinear point; keeping collinear points with < 0; sorting by bitrate only, so a lower score at the same bitrate enters the stack first; not stopping at the lowest bitrate with the best score, which adds a flat or falling tail; resolving duplicates numerically instead of as strings; scanning the full list per title; for the budget, computing every rung's area once and removing the k smallest without updating neighbours.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A point below the hull is beaten by switching between its neighbours over time, which averages to a point on the chord with the same bitrate and better quality. A product may still want a specific resolution for a device class or a minimum-bandwidth rung, as a constraint added after pruning. (2) A minimum ratio between neighbours makes the choice a constrained selection; greedy from the top can be suboptimal, and a DP over the hull points sorted by bitrate (best area with i rungs ending at j) is exact. (3) Prune per codec and keep ladders separate per codec family, so a device gets a complete ladder for the codec it supports; during migration, publish both and switch per device capability. (4) Noise can promote or demote rungs near the hull. Use repeated measurements or confidence bands, require a margin above the chord, and keep ladders stable across runs unless the change is material.

Rubric anchors. 2: a correct idea with floating-point slopes or a missing tie rule; several edge tests fail. 3: all tests pass with a sort and a monotone stack and exact integer tests. 4: also explains why dominance and the stack together give exactly the definition, handles the budget with updated neighbours, and answers the noise or codec follow-up concretely.

Strong signals. Asks how collinear points and equal scores are treated before coding; reaches for the cross product immediately. Red flags. Rounding scores to make ties go away; a quadratic or cubic algorithm defended as "titles are small" without looking at the input size.

from fractions import Fraction


def top10(rows, titles, day, country=None, k=10):
    # the latest delivery of the day's viewing, per country
    latest = {}
    for r in rows:
        if r["day"] == day:
            latest[r["country"]] = max(latest.get(r["country"], 0), r["batch"])

    seconds = {}
    for r in rows:
        if r["day"] != day or r["kind"] != "play":
            continue
        if country is not None and r["country"] != country:
            continue
        if r["batch"] != latest[r["country"]]:
            continue
        seconds[r["title"]] = seconds.get(r["title"], 0) + r["seconds"]

    ranked = []
    for title, secs in seconds.items():
        info = titles.get(title)
        if info is None or info.get("runtime_min") is None:
            continue
        exact = Fraction(secs, info["runtime_min"] * 60)      # views, compared exactly
        ranked.append((exact, title, secs / 3600, secs / (info["runtime_min"] * 60)))

    ranked.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], x[1]))
    out = []
    rank = 0
    for i, (exact, title, hours, views) in enumerate(ranked[:k]):
        if i == 0 or exact != ranked[i - 1][0]:
            rank = i + 1                                       # 1, 2, 2, 4
        out.append((rank, title, hours, views))
    return out

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. The latest batch is chosen per day, not per day and country. latest is keyed by r["day"], so a restatement in one country (batch 2) makes every other country's batch-1 rows look stale. Symptom: a country's list is empty, or the global list loses most countries, on a day another country was restated. Fix: key by country (the day is already fixed), as latest[r["country"]], and look it up the same way.
  2. The preview filter compares with "previews". The data says "preview", so previews are counted as viewing. Symptom: titles whose trailers autoplay on the home page climb the list. Fix: count only kind == "play" (or compare with "preview"); counting only the allowed kind is safer than excluding a known one.
  3. Runtime hours use integer division. runtime_min // 60 turns 90 minutes into 1 hour, so views are 1.5 times too high, and a runtime under an hour would divide by zero. Symptom: a 90-minute film's views come out too high. Fix: runtime_min / 60.
  4. The list is ordered by hours, not views. The sort key is x[1], the hours. Symptom: long seasons with many hours rank above short films with more views. Fix: sort by views, then title id.
  5. Ranks are positions. i + 1 gives 1, 2, 3, 4 for tied views. Symptom: two titles with identical views get different ranks. Fix: a competition rank, which keeps the previous rank while views are equal, comparing exactly.

Each bug has its own check that the others pass: a restatement in another country, a preview row, a 90-minute runtime, a 60-minute title against a 180-minute one, and three-way views with a tie. The samples usually fail on several bugs at once. The checks for a full replacement by a restated delivery, a tie at the cut, the global list, titles missing from the catalogue and other days pass on the original code: they guard against fixes that break those rules.

Explanation. Views are a ratio of two integers: seconds over runtime seconds. The reference compares them exactly as fractions, which is what the specification means by "compare exactly". Computing them as seconds / (runtime_min * 60) in floating point also keeps ties for the sizes here, because equal fractions of exactly representable integers round to the same float; computing (seconds / 3600) / (runtime_min / 60) rounds twice and can split a tie of fractions written differently, so a strong candidate notices that and either cross-multiplies or uses the single division.

Complexity. O(n) over rows plus O(t log t) to sort t titles. The timing test is 200 000 rows and 3 000 titles, about 0.1 s.

Dialect notes. In SQL the restatement rule is batch = MAX(batch) OVER (PARTITION BY day, country) (partitioning by day only is bug 1 in SQL form), and the rank is RANK() OVER (ORDER BY views DESC); DENSE_RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 3 and ROW_NUMBER gives positions (bug 5). Integer division is the default for integer / integer in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, so bug 3 appears in SQL as runtime_min / 60; Snowflake, BigQuery and Spark SQL return a decimal or float there. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A restatement in another country; a restated delivery that drops a title; previews; a 90-minute runtime; views against hours; a three-way tie in views; a tie at the cut; the global list; a title missing from the catalogue and one with no runtime; viewing on other days; a 200 000-row timing check.

Common mistakes. Fixing bug 1 by taking the latest batch per row or per title, which keeps a title that a restatement removed; normalising strings to hide the preview typo instead of filtering on the allowed kind; switching to DENSE_RANK-style ranks; rounding views before comparing; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Publish a version and a timestamp with every list; a correction is a new version with a change note, and partners get the diff. (2) In this exercise a season's runtime is the sum of its episodes as of the day; adding an episode lowers views for the same hours, so the rule must say which runtime applies (as of the viewing day is the defensible choice). (3) Keep a per-day, per-country, per-title aggregate; a restated delivery replaces one country-day partition and the lists are re-ranked from aggregates. (4) Either show both titles and let the list run to eleven, or break the tie by a published rule; the decision belongs to whoever owns the published methodology, not to the pipeline.

NFX-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Event identity and schema. Every event carries device_id, profile_id, session_id (chosen by the app at playback start), a per-session seq that increases by one, the event type, the playback position, the device's wall-clock time, the device's monotonic time since boot and a boot_id. The identity of an event is (device_id, session_id, seq). Heartbeats carry the cumulative seconds played in the session, so a missing heartbeat loses no viewing.
  • Edge ingestion. Regional endpoints authenticate the device, validate the schema, stamp the server receive time and write the batch to the regional durable log before acknowledging. The device deletes events from its buffer only after the acknowledgement. Per-device and per-region rate limits return a retry-after, and replays from offline buffers are marked so they can be throttled separately from live traffic.
  • Durable log. Partitioned by device_id (or session_id), so a session stays in order within one partition and load spreads evenly; no partition key based on title or country, which would be hot. Live and replay traffic can go to separate topics with separate consumer quotas.
  • Deduplication. A stream processor keyed by session keeps the highest contiguous seq and a small set of seen sequence numbers per open session in a state store, with a retention longer than the offline window ({{offline_window}} plus margin). Events for sessions older than that are checked against the historical store by key in the batch layer. Identity is assigned by the device, so retries are exact duplicates.
  • Time correction. When a device is online, offset = receive_time - device_time is estimated from recent requests (the minimum over a window approximates network delay). For buffered events, the time is reconstructed from the monotonic clock: event_time = upload_receive_time - (upload_monotonic - event_monotonic) within the same boot_id. If the boot changed or the clock is implausible (before the device's first registration, in the future), the event keeps its order within the session and is placed using the session's other events, flagged as estimated.
  • Consumers. Resume points read the live stream with a seconds-level SLA and last-writer-wins by (session, seq), ignoring replayed events older than the current resume point unless they are newer by sequence. Viewing history is an upsert by session. Popularity counts are computed in batch by event day from the deduplicated table, with a lateness policy and restatements. Quality monitoring uses receive time windows and tolerates loss.
  • Storage. The deduplicated events land in an append-only table partitioned by event date and region, with a late-arrival partition column so that late data for a past day is visible and countable.
  • Health metrics. Ingest rate by region and platform, acknowledgement latency, duplicate rate per app version, share of events with corrected or estimated time, late-event volume by days late, consumer lag, rejected events by reason.

Competing designs to accept. Deduplicating in the batch layer only (simpler; resume points then need their own idempotent upsert); a session-windowed stream job that emits one record per session (strong for counts, weaker for resume points); using server receive time only and accepting distortion for offline viewing (acceptable only if the candidate quantifies it and keeps device time for later correction).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Reconnect storms after outages; hot partitions keyed by title; unbounded dedup state; clock resets producing events decades in the past; deleted history items reappearing from replay; acknowledgement before the durable write losing events in a regional failure.

Incident guidance.

  • Reconnect storm: the replay topic absorbs the burst while live traffic keeps its quota; per-device retry-after spreads the uploads; consumers of the replay topic scale out; resume points ignore replayed events older than the current position. Watch replay lag, not just ingest rate.
  • Clock reset to 2000: implausible timestamps are detected (before registration, before the app version existed); events are re-timed from the monotonic clock and the receive time within the boot; popularity counts are not polluted with a day in 2000. Report the affected device family to the device team.
  • Retry bug, 30% duplicates: deduplication by (device, session, seq) removes them; the duplicate-rate monitor per app version alerts; the ingestion cost rises, so throttle that app version and fix the client.

Follow-up guidance. (1) As in the storm incident: throttling with retry-after, a separate replay path, per-stage lag, and nothing acknowledged before it is durable. (2) Events after the jump within one boot keep the monotonic clock, so their spacing is right; re-anchor them to the last good offset. (3) Count them into the event day by a published rule: recompute the day with a restatement, or count them into a late bucket; never into the arrival day silently. (4) Per-device sequence numbers allow a gap audit: compare the acknowledged high-water marks the devices report against the stored maximum contiguous sequence per session. (5) Cost per event per platform and app version on a dashboard with a budget alert; server-side sampling or an adaptive heartbeat interval.

Rubric anchors. 2: events identified by a random id or not at all, only server time, a single path for all consumers. 3: device-assigned identity with dedup, a durable acknowledgement, a session-preserving partition key, device and server time with a correction rule, separate lateness handling per consumer. 4: also monotonic-clock reconstruction across offline periods, reconnect-storm controls, an auditable no-loss argument, and credible incident handling.

Strong signals. Asks how long devices buffer before choosing the dedup window; separates live and replay traffic. Red flags. "Use the device timestamp" with no correction; acknowledging before the write is durable.

NFX-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Inputs. Deduplicated playback sessions (from the ingestion pipeline), versioned by delivery: each daily delivery per country carries a version, and a re-delivery is a new version, never an overwrite. The catalogue's runtimes and season structure are a slowly changing table with effective dates (SCD type 2). The definition of what counts as viewing (title playback; not previews or trailers) is applied at this boundary.
  • Daily aggregate. title_day_country (event_day, country, title_id, seconds_played, sessions, input_versions, run_id), rebuilt per (event_day, country) partition by overwrite. Views are computed in a separate step: views = seconds / runtime_seconds_as_of(event_day), with runtime joined as of the viewing day. Seasons use the sum of their episodes' runtimes as of that day. A runtime of zero or null fails the check, it does not divide.
  • Lateness and restatements. Every day is recomputed each night for {{late_window}} after it ends, cheaply, from the late partitions only. Viewing arriving after {{late_window}} is counted into its event day in a monthly reconciliation run, not into the published daily list, and the difference is reported.
  • Publication. A published_list (list_date, country, version, published_at, rank, title_id, hours, views, run_id) table. The first version is published at {{publish_at}}. A later version is published only when a rule says so (for example, a change in membership of the list or more than a set percentage in a published number), with a change note. Ranks use competition ranking; ties at the cut are shown by a published rule.
  • Small numbers. Country-title figures below a minimum audience are suppressed, and the global figure is published only rounded or only for titles above a threshold in enough countries, so suppressed values cannot be recovered by subtraction.
  • Checks before publication. Completeness per country (delivery arrived, row count within band), runtime sanity (no zero, no sudden change), day-over-day change limits per title, sum of country hours against the global total, and a diff against the previous version. A failed check holds that country's list, not every list.
  • Reproducibility. Each run records input versions, catalogue snapshot and code version; a backfill for a past day with the same inputs gives the same output.

Competing designs to accept. A streaming aggregation with daily snapshots (fine if snapshots are immutable and restatements are explicit); publishing provisional numbers and a final version after {{late_window}} (fine with clear labels); a warehouse-native pipeline with snapshot tables. Any is fine with versioned inputs, explicit publication and a late-data policy.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Appending a re-delivered day; runtime joined as of today instead of the viewing day; a zero runtime; global lists computed by summing country ranks instead of aggregates; late data silently shifting published numbers; suppressed cells recoverable from totals.

Incident guidance.

  • Re-delivery of two published days: land as new versions; recompute both days for that country; diff against the published versions; republish only if the rule is met, with a change note; tell partners which numbers changed.
  • Runtime set to 0: the runtime check fails for that title; hold that title (or the country lists containing it) and use the last valid runtime only if the methodology allows it; fix the catalogue; rerun. Never publish an infinite or missing view count.
  • Late holiday viewing understates by 12%: expected for offline-heavy periods; the provisional label or the republication rule handles it; measure the late share by day of week and holiday, and consider a later first publication for those days.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Recompute every day in the affected week with the corrected runtime; republish under the rule with a change note; partners receive the diff. (2) Each choice is defensible with a policy: publish once with a known understatement, publish provisional then final, or delay; the strong answer uses measured late shares. (3) Competition rank with a rule for ties at the cut; the same rule everywhere unless the methodology says otherwise. (4) Time goes to the joins with sessions and the per-country ranking; make the aggregate incremental by partition and re-rank from aggregates. (5) The global list is ranked on global views, not on the sum of country ranks; it equals the sum of country hours unless suppression or late data differ between them, which is the bug to look for.

Rubric anchors. 2: a daily append of aggregates; runtime from the current catalogue; no publication versioning. 3: versioned inputs, partition overwrite, runtime as of the day, publication separate from computation with versions, a late-data policy. 4: also suppression that resists subtraction, pre-publication checks per country, reproducible backfills, and incident handling with partner communication.

Strong signals. Separates "computed" from "published"; asks which runtime applies to a season with new episodes. Red flags. "We fix the numbers in place"; dividing by runtime with no guard.

NFX-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • What a title is.
    • titles (title_id, kind film|series, original_language, first_release_date); seasons (season_id, title_id, season_no); episodes (episode_id, season_id, episode_no). A film has no season or episode rows; a "playable unit" is a film or an episode (unit_id with a kind, or a nullable episode on a common table).
    • title_localisations (title_id, language, name, synopsis, artwork_ref, valid_from, recorded_at): localised metadata as versioned rows; a missing language falls back to a stated default.
  • What can be played.
    • versions (version_id, unit_id, cut original|edited, runtime_s, published_at): immutable; a corrected encode or an edited cut is a new version.
    • audio_tracks (version_id, language, type original|dub|audio_description, published_at, withdrawn_at) and subtitle_tracks (version_id, language, type subtitles|closed_captions|forced_narrative, published_at, withdrawn_at). Tracks belong to a version, never to a title.
    • version_assignment (unit_id, country, version_id, valid_from, valid_to): which cut a country gets.
  • Where and when.
    • licences (licence_id, title_id, scope seasons[] or film, countries[], signed_at) normalised into availability_windows (window_id, licence_id, title_id, season_id NULL, country, start_utc, end_utc, valid_from_recorded, valid_to_recorded): one row per (licence, season or film, country). Half-open [start_utc, end_utc), computed from local midnight in the country's catalogue time zone when the window is recorded (store the local date and zone too, so a zone-rule change can be re-derived).
    • Bitemporal history. A change never updates a row in place: it closes the old row's recorded interval (valid_to_recorded = now) and inserts the new one. "What was playable at T" reads rows current now with start_utc ≤ T < end_utc; "what did we believe on D about T" reads rows with valid_from_recorded ≤ D < valid_to_recorded.
  • Availability check for (episode, country, T): exists a window for the episode's title and (its season or the whole title) in that country with start_utc ≤ T < end_utc, AND the country's assigned version at T exists and has at least one audio track published by T. Overlapping windows from two licences are fine (an exists test, not a sum).
  • Facts.
    • fct_availability_day (title_id, season_id, country, date, is_available, available_hours): derived from windows by expanding intervals to days for the affected (title, country) pairs only; rebuilt incrementally from the change log (each window change names the dates and pairs to recompute).
    • fct_track_coverage_day (country, date, language, track_type, available_hours_with_track, available_hours): answers the dub/subtitle share; derived from availability × versions × tracks.
    • Arrivals and departures: windows whose start_utc or end_utc falls in the next month, from current rows, with the local date for display.

Competing designs to accept. Windows at episode grain (simpler checks, many more rows) if the expansion is derived from licences. A single interval table keyed by (unit, country) produced by a rights system, treated as the source, with history kept as an append-only change log rather than bitemporal columns. Range types with exclusion constraints in PostgreSQL to forbid inconsistent overlaps within one licence. Storing the localised metadata in a document store, if keys and versions remain.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Inclusive end dates and local/UTC confusion (off-by-one day in every country); tracks attached at title level; overwriting windows (history lost, past reports drift); full daily rebuild of title × country × day across {{countries}} countries (expensive at {{titles}} titles; do it incrementally); forgetting that a country can get an edited cut whose tracks differ.

Incident guidance.

  • Season stayed playable one day after the licence ended: the end was loaded as inclusive. Contain by correcting the windows (new rows, not edits) and invalidating the availability cache; quantify exposure from plays in [intended_end, loaded_end) per country — the list rights asked for. Fix at the boundary: one loader converts local dates to half-open UTC intervals, with a contract test on a known licence; add a daily check that no play occurs outside a current window.
  • Dub offered for every season: tracks were attached at series level by a tool. Contain by withdrawing the series-level mapping and regenerating the per-version track list; quantify affected plays (audio language chosen ≠ audio track served). Guard with a constraint that tracks reference a version, and a pre-publish check that every advertised language exists on the version for that country.
  • Bulk overwrite changed last quarter's numbers: history was edited in place. Restore the prior state from backups or the change log into the bitemporal table; reproduce the reported numbers with "as recorded on" reads; make writes insert-only (revoke UPDATE on the window table, or route all changes through a procedure that closes and inserts). With about {{window_changes}} changes a week, an append-only log is small.

Follow-up guidance. (1) EXISTS over windows for the title with season = the episode's season or NULL (whole title), country, half-open test; plus the version/track test. (2) Store end_utc = local midnight converted (05:00 UTC next day for UTC−5); the daily fact must say which "day" it uses (country-local date is the natural choice). (3) Recompute only the (title, country, date range) pairs named by each change; a nightly full check for drift is fine. (4) Bitemporal read with recorded ≤ 1 March for the plan and current rows for the actual; diff the two. (5) The corrected file is a new track row (or a new version), the old one withdrawn with a reason; audits see both.

Rubric anchors. 2: one titles table with an "available countries" list or flag, tracks on the title, no history. 3: hierarchy, versions with tracks, windows at season/country grain with half-open intervals, a correct availability check and a daily fact. 4: also bitemporal history (actual versus believed), the local-midnight conversion, edited cuts per country, incremental facts and a convincing account of each incident.

Strong signals. Asks at which level a licence applies before drawing tables; states the interval convention unprompted; separates "what we believed" from "what was". Red flags. Availability as a boolean column; dubs as an array on the title; end dates stored as inclusive local dates with no time zone.

NFX-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Entities and history.
    • accounts (account_id, country, created_at); account_plans (account_id, plan_id, valid_from, valid_to) (the plan history itself is modelled in the subscription domain).
    • profiles (profile_id, created_at, type standard|kids, deleted_at NULL); profile_settings_history (profile_id, maturity_ceiling, language, valid_from, valid_to).
    • profile_membership (profile_id, account_id, valid_from, valid_to, reason created|transferred): a profile's account is an interval, so a transfer closes one row and opens another.
    • extra_members (member_id, host_account_id, login_id, country, valid_from, valid_to): an extra member has their own login and profile(s) and is billed through the host account.
    • devices (device_id, device_type, first_seen_at); device_signins (device_id, account_id, signed_in_at, signed_out_at).
    • household_assignments (account_id, household_id, device_id, valid_from, valid_to, confidence, method): coarse placement only; no precise location is stored, and raw network signals are kept briefly (days) and then dropped.
  • Plays. plays (play_id, profile_id, account_id_at_play, device_id, household_id_at_play, in_primary_household, extra_member_id NULL, maturity_ceiling_at_play, started_at, ended_at, title_id, episode_id). Attribution is frozen at play time: the profile selected, and the account and household that held it then. It never changes after the fact, so published metrics are stable without restatement logic.
  • Transfer. Close profile_membership, open a new row on the new account. The profile's history moves with the profile id (personalisation reads by profile). Account-level metrics read account_id_at_play and do not change; any "current owner" view is a separate, labelled lens.
  • Deletion. deleted_at set; a deletion job, within the stated deadline (for example 30 days), removes the profile's plays from personalisation stores and raw row-level tables (or replaces the profile id with a tombstone key unlinkable to the account), drops it from the next training snapshot, and records completion per store. Published aggregates keep their counts. Snapshots older than the deadline are expired by retention, not edited.
  • Kids profiles. Row-level kids data lives in a restricted schema used only by that profile's personalisation; analytics read pre-aggregated facts (by maturity rating, country, day) with a minimum count per cell and no profile ids. Access is granted by role and audited.
  • Facts. fct_profile_activity_month (profile_id_hash, account_id_at_play, month, minutes, active); fct_kids_minutes_day (country, date, maturity_rating, minutes, profiles_bucketed) with thresholds; fct_plays_household_day (account segment, date, plays, plays_outside_primary); "active" defined (for example ≥ 1 play of ≥ 60 s in the month).

Competing designs to accept. Looking attribution up through interval joins instead of copying it onto the play, if every lookup is as-of the play time and the cost is understood. Modelling extra members as a special profile type (if billing and login separation are clear). A separate identity graph service. Hard deletion of raw plays versus pseudonymisation, with the trade-off for aggregates explained.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Current-state joins that rewrite history; "user" conflated with profile or account; kids data in general tables; deletion that misses copies (snapshots, features, exports); household signals stored at high precision indefinitely; volume: at {{daily_plays}} plays a day, interval joins at query time are expensive, which is one more argument for freezing attribution at ingestion.

Incident guidance.

  • TV release defaulted to the first profile: attribution was wrong at the source, so freezing it preserved the error. Contain by fixing the client and flagging the affected device/app version and window; repair personalisation (reset or down-weight those plays for the affected profiles) and annotate the metrics for the week rather than guessing the right profile. Guard: a play must carry an explicit profile-selection event id; monitor the share of plays per device on the first profile after releases.
  • Active accounts changed on every rebuild after transfers: plays were joined to the current account. Rebuild from account_id_at_play (or as-of interval joins), compare against what finance used, and publish one documented restatement if they differ. Guard with a test that a closed month's metric is identical across two rebuilds.
  • Household placement change tripled outside-household plays: a method change moved a device family to a new household id. Record method and version on assignments, compare the metric by method, roll back or re-baseline, and gate any enforcement or communication on a stable metric. With about {{devices_per_household}} devices per household, one device family is a large share of plays.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Copied: profile, account at play, household at play, device, maturity ceiling at play; looked up: device type, title metadata. (2) A new membership row; old plays keep account_id_at_play; last year's report unchanged. (3) Aggregates by rating, country and day with minimum cell sizes and no profile-level output. (4) Raw plays: delete or tombstone; features: purge; last week's snapshot: excluded from the next one and expired by retention; published aggregates: unchanged. (5) Denormalise the at-play attributes; a mid-month household change is just two intervals, and plays carry whichever was in force.

Rubric anchors. 2: one users table, profile's current account joined at query time, no deletion or kids story. 3: distinct entities with interval history, attribution frozen on the play, a working transfer and deletion path. 4: also kids-profile governance with thresholds, coarse household signals with retention, stable published metrics, and incident repair that does not guess.

Strong signals. Refuses to call a profile a person; separates personalisation data from published aggregates when discussing deletion. Red flags. Storing precise location; kids plays in a general table with ad hoc filters; rewriting history on transfer.

NFX-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Source. source_versions (source_version_id, unit_id, picture_lock_at, supersedes_id, change_summary): each editorial re-cut is a new source version; source_change_map (optional) records which timecode ranges changed, so conform needs can be computed.
  • Orders. work_orders (work_order_id, unit_id, language, deliverable_type subtitles|cc|forced|dub|audio_description, source_version_id, ordered_at, needed_by_launch_id); work_order_assignments (work_order_id, vendor_id, assigned_at, unassigned_at).
  • Deliveries. deliveries (delivery_id, work_order_id, vendor_id, source_version_id_claimed, checksum, storage_ref, uploaded_at): immutable; uniqueness on (work_order_id, checksum) collapses duplicate uploads to one delivery (or a duplicate_of link).
  • Checks. qc_runs (qc_run_id, delivery_id, checked_against_source_version_id, check_suite_version, started_at, outcome pass|fail); qc_findings (qc_run_id, severity, type timing|reading_speed|format|translation|mix, timecode_in, timecode_out, note).
  • Decisions. approvals (work_order_id, delivery_id, source_version_id, decided_at, decision approved|rejected, reviewer_role).
  • Due dates. launches (launch_id, unit_or_title, country, launch_at, valid_from, valid_to) (history); due_dates (work_order_id, due_at, computed_at, reason) recomputed whenever a relevant launch changes: earliest launch among countries needing the language minus a lead time per type. Both the due date at assignment and the current one are kept.
  • Derived status (view over events): no delivery → ordered/overdue; latest delivery without a QC run → in QC; latest QC failed → failed (awaiting re-delivery); approved for the current source version → approved; approved only for an older source version → needs conform; reassigned → back to ordered for the new vendor.
  • Invariant. A work order is complete only if an approval exists for source_version_id = current source version of the unit.
  • Facts. fct_delivery (delivery grain: vendor, language, type, attempt_no, qc outcome, dates); fct_work_order (work-order grain: first-pass pass flag, cycle time order→approval, on-time vs due at assignment and vs current due); at-risk view: incomplete work orders with due date or launch within 14 days. Vendors read row-filtered views by vendor_id.

Competing designs to accept. An event log of deliverable state transitions with status as a projection. Storing the due date only at assignment plus a separate "current due" view. One table of "assets" with a type column for deliveries and source versions, if the version references stay explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A mutable status column (loses failures, yield unmeasurable); files overwritten (unreviewable QC); QC that does not record the source version it checked against; due dates copied once; duplicate uploads counted as attempts; vendor views built by copying data per vendor. At {{titles_per_month}} launches × {{languages}} languages × several types, work orders number in the tens to hundreds of thousands a month — modest — but QC findings per timecode are larger; keep them at full grain for a limited time.

Incident guidance.

  • Re-cut after approval; QC passed against the old source: approvals and QC were not tied to the current source version. Contain by pulling or flagging the out-of-sync subtitles in affected countries and re-opening the work orders as "needs conform"; fix QC to always check against the unit's current source version and record it; add the completeness invariant (approval for the current source version) to the launch gate. Impact scales with {{languages}} languages.
  • Every upload arrived twice; yield halved: duplicates were counted as attempts. Collapse by (work order, checksum), recompute yield, and tell the vendor's manager which numbers were wrong. Guard with the uniqueness rule and a monitor on duplicate checksum rate per vendor.
  • Launch moved earlier; at-risk report stayed green: due dates were copied at assignment. Recompute due dates from launch history, re-run the at-risk report, escalate the real risks, and keep both due dates so the vendor is judged fairly (on the date they were given, with the change noted).

Follow-up guidance. (1) Status as a function of the latest delivery, its QC, approvals and the current source version (state machine in a view). (2) Judge on the due date in force when the order was placed or last accepted, and report against the current one separately. (3) A new source version row; approvals for the old one stop satisfying the invariant; work orders with timed deliverables in changed ranges go to "needs conform"; the at-risk report picks them up. (4) Row-level security or per-vendor views filtered by vendor_id; never copies. (5) Delivery and finding grain for months; work-order facts for years.

Rubric anchors. 2: one deliverables table with a status column and a due date. 3: orders, immutable deliveries, QC runs with findings, approvals and derived status with clear yield/on-time definitions. 4: also source versions in the key of approvals, conform logic, due-date history from launches, duplicate detection and vendor-scoped access.

Strong signals. Asks how a re-cut affects approved work before designing tables; defines first-pass yield precisely. Red flags. Overwriting files; status as the only record; ignoring the source version.

NFX-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Price list. plans (plan_id, streams, quality, has_ads); plan_prices (plan_id, country, currency, amount_minor, effective_from, effective_to, announced_at): effective-dated, never updated in place.
  • Subscription and plan history (SCD type 2). subscriptions (subscription_id, member_id, country, currency, billing_channel direct|partner, partner_id NULL, partner_subscriber_ref NULL, started_at); subscription_plan_history (subscription_id, plan_id, price_amount_minor, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, change_reason upgrade|downgrade|price_change|partner_message): one row per period in which plan and price are constant. The price is copied onto the row from the price list using the notice rule, so the row states what the member pays.
  • Price change rule. For each member: new price from the first billing date on or after the effective date, provided the member was notified at least {{notice_days}} days before that billing date (otherwise from the next billing date). Encoded in the job that writes the SCD rows, with the notice record (price_notices (member_id, change_id, notified_at)) as input.
  • State machine. subscription_states (subscription_id, state active|on_hold|paused|cancelling|ended, valid_from, valid_to, reason): transitions with timestamps. Cancel → "cancelling" with access until period end → ended. Payment failure → on hold; success within {{retry_days}} days → active (no churn); otherwise ended with reason involuntary.
  • Billing. billing_periods (subscription_id, period_start, period_end, plan_id, amount_minor); invoices; payment_attempts (invoice_id, attempt_no, attempted_at, outcome, decline_code).
  • Partner feed. partner_messages (partner_id, message_id, partner_subscriber_ref, type activate|change|deactivate, plan_id, effective_at, received_at) with uniqueness on (partner_id, message_id); applied in effective_at order per subscriber, idempotently; reconciled daily against the partner's billing file.
  • Facts. fct_membership_day built from intervals (or a monthly snapshot plus intervals): state, plan, price per subscription per day for the window needed; as-of queries via interval joins (valid_from ≤ d < valid_to). fct_membership_movements_day: gross adds (new subscriptions), rejoins (new subscription for a member who ended earlier), voluntary churn (ended after cancel), involuntary churn (ended after hold expiry); identity: active(d) = active(d−1) + gross adds + rejoins − voluntary − involuntary ± pause transitions (stated). Revenue per currency in minor units; conversion for global totals at a stated rate table.

Competing designs to accept. An event-sourced subscription (events as the record, SCD as a projection). Keeping price outside the SCD row and joining to the price list with the notice rule at query time (correct but harder to audit). Monthly snapshots plus change intervals instead of daily facts. Paused as a flag on active rather than a state, if the churn and revenue rules are explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Price changes dated by effective date only; plan as a column overwritten; churn counted at hold start; partner duplicates and out-of-order messages; mixing currencies; daily snapshots of {{members}} members kept forever.

Incident guidance.

  • Price applied from the effective date to everyone: the notice and billing-date rule was not encoded. Recompute the SCD rows for affected members from the price list, notices and billing dates; restate recurring revenue for the affected days with a note; check whether any member was actually billed early (that is a customer issue, not only a report issue) and refund. Guard with a test that no member's price changes before their first billing date on or after the effective date with {{notice_days}} days' notice.
  • Partner resent a month of activations: messages were not idempotent. Deduplicate by (partner, message id) — and by (partner, subscriber ref, effective time, type) where ids changed — close the duplicate subscriptions, recompute gross adds for that partner, and reconcile to the partner's file. With about {{partner_share}} of members billed by partners, one partner's replay is a visible share of daily adds.
  • Recovered holds counted as churn and re-acquisition: churn was recorded at hold start or before the retry window ended. Recompute movements with churn only when the {{retry_days}}-day window ends without payment; restate the month; add a test that a hold followed by a payment produces no churn and no gross add.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Rows: plan A until the 10th, plan B from the 10th, paused state from the 20th (plan row unchanged or closed, as stated), resumed, then plan C from the next billing date. (2) Members whose billing date in the month is on or after the effective date and who were notified in time pay the new price from that date; revenue on the 15th uses each member's row in force on the 15th. (3) Definitions as above; the identity must hold to the member. (4) Uniqueness on message id, ordering by effective time, last-writer-wins by effective time with a sequence tiebreak, daily reconciliation. (5) Intervals as the source; a monthly snapshot for fast scans plus intervals for days between; partitions by month of valid_from.

Rubric anchors. 2: a subscriptions table with current plan and status, churn as cancellations. 3: SCD type 2 plan history, effective-dated prices, a state machine with on hold and paused, partner messages deduplicated. 4: also the notice and billing-date rule encoded, a net-adds identity that handles recovery, rejoins and pauses, currency discipline, and as-of serving without unbounded snapshots.

Strong signals. Distinguishes voluntary from involuntary churn and recovery without prompting; treats the partner file as the reconciliation source. Red flags. Updating plan or price in place; summing amounts across currencies; counting every hold as churn.

NFX-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{gap_minutes}}, {{min_episodes}} and {{min_view_s}} are the instance's values — {{min_view_s}} is 0 at Medium, where every play is a view)

WITH dedup AS (                                -- one row per play_id: the feed may redeliver
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (play_id) play_id, profile_id, title_id, episode_id, started_at, ended_at, start_reason
  FROM plays
  ORDER BY play_id, received_at
), views AS (                                  -- the end of a play whose stop event was lost
  SELECT d.play_id, d.profile_id, d.title_id, d.episode_id, e.season_no, d.started_at, d.start_reason,
         COALESCE(d.ended_at, d.started_at + e.runtime_min * INTERVAL '1 minute') AS ended_at
  FROM dedup d
  LEFT JOIN episodes e ON e.episode_id = d.episode_id
), kept AS (                                   -- false starts are not views
  SELECT * FROM views
  WHERE ended_at - started_at >= {{min_view_s}} * INTERVAL '1 second'
), flagged AS (
  SELECT k.*,
         CASE WHEN k.episode_id IS NOT NULL
               AND LAG(k.episode_id) OVER w IS NOT NULL
               AND LAG(k.title_id)   OVER w = k.title_id
               AND LAG(k.season_no)  OVER w = k.season_no
               AND k.started_at - LAG(k.ended_at) OVER w <= {{gap_minutes}} * INTERVAL '1 minute'
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_session
  FROM kept k
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY k.profile_id ORDER BY k.started_at, k.play_id)
), numbered AS (
  SELECT f.*, SUM(f.new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY f.profile_id ORDER BY f.started_at, f.play_id) AS session_no
  FROM flagged f
), sessions AS (
  SELECT profile_id, session_no,
         MIN(title_id) AS title_id, MIN(season_no) AS season_no,
         COUNT(DISTINCT episode_id) AS episodes,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE new_session = 0 AND start_reason = 'autoplay') AS autoplay_cont,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE new_session = 0 AND start_reason = 'chosen')   AS chosen_cont
  FROM numbered
  WHERE episode_id IS NOT NULL                 -- a film is a session of its own and never a binge
  GROUP BY profile_id, session_no
)
SELECT t.title_name, s.season_no,
       COUNT(*)                     AS binge_sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.profile_id) AS binge_profiles,
       SUM(s.episodes)              AS episodes_in_binges,
       SUM(s.autoplay_cont)         AS autoplay_continuations,
       SUM(s.chosen_cont)           AS chosen_continuations
FROM sessions s
JOIN titles t ON t.title_id = s.title_id
WHERE s.episodes >= {{min_episodes}}
GROUP BY t.title_name, s.season_no
ORDER BY t.title_name, s.season_no;

Explanation. This is gaps and islands over each profile's whole viewing sequence. Views are cleaned first — one row per play_id (Very Hard), the missing end derived from the episode's runtime (Very Hard), plays shorter than the view threshold dropped (Hard and up) — because "the view immediately before" must be computed over views, not raw rows. A view continues a session only if it and the previous view are episodes of the same title and season and the gap from the previous ended_at is at most the threshold; any NULL in that test (a film before or after) falls to the ELSE branch and starts a session. A running SUM of the start flag numbers sessions; each session belongs to exactly one (title, season) because the continuation rule requires both to match, so MIN() simply reads them. Distinct episodes decide the threshold and feed episodes_in_binges; continuations are the views with new_session = 0, so a session's first view is never one, even when it was autoplayed from a previous season's finale.

Complexity. One sort of the cleaned plays by (profile, started_at, play_id) for both window functions (they share the ordering), then hash aggregates per session and per (title, season). In production the sort is per profile partition and sessions are computed incrementally with a look-back of the gap threshold into the previous day.

Dialect notes. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL; Snowflake and BigQuery use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY play_id ORDER BY received_at) = 1, Spark SQL and MySQL 8 a subquery on the row number. COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) is PostgreSQL (and Spark SQL 3.x); elsewhere use SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) or COUNT_IF (Snowflake, BigQuery). Interval arithmetic differs: DATEDIFF('second', prev_end, started_at) <= 60 * N in Snowflake (counts boundaries crossed, so compare in seconds, not minutes), TIMESTAMP_DIFF(started_at, prev_end, SECOND) in BigQuery, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …) in MySQL, unix_timestamp differences in Spark; TIMESTAMPADD/DATEADD for the runtime end. A named WINDOW clause is not available in every engine; repeat the OVER clause. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data.
